name: DeepScribe
summary: Ambient AI medical scribe that listens to clinician–patient visits and generates structured notes directly into the EHR, designed to reduce after-hours charting and documentation burden.
description: DeepScribe is an ambient AI medical scribe for clinicians. It securely listens to clinician–patient conversations (in-person or virtual), transcribes the encounter, and generates structured clinical notes that can be reviewed and signed in the EHR. The goal is to reduce after-hours charting and administrative burden so clinicians can focus more on patients. DeepScribe is used across primary care and multiple specialties and is designed to be HIPAA-compliant, with Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) and controls to prevent recorded PHI from being used to train general-purpose models. It is a clinician-facing workflow tool, not a diagnostic or treatment app for patients.
patient_summary: DeepScribe is an AI medical scribe for clinicians, not an app for patients. Your doctor may use DeepScribe to record your visit (with your permission) so that the computer can write the medical note for them. The clinician then reviews and signs the note in the chart. The goal is to reduce how much time clinicians spend typing so they can focus more on you during the visit. DeepScribe does not make diagnoses, prescribe medications, or replace your clinician’s judgment.

sections.heading: What DeepScribe Does
sections.text: DeepScribe is an ambient AI medical scribe that listens to clinician–patient conversations (with consent) and turns them into structured clinical notes. During the visit, the clinician can focus on the patient while DeepScribe captures the conversation and generates a draft note in the background. After the encounter, the clinician reviews, edits if needed, and signs the note in the EHR. DeepScribe is designed to reduce documentation time, decrease after-hours charting, and support more consistent note structure without replacing clinical judgment.

sections.heading: How Well Does It Work?
sections.comparison: Reported workflow burden with vs. without ambient scribe tools
sections.text: Early case studies and vendor-reported outcomes suggest that ambient AI scribes like DeepScribe can reduce the amount of time clinicians spend writing notes after visits and may cut down on evening and weekend charting. Some clinics report substantial decreases in time spent per note and higher clinician satisfaction with documentation. However, these data are primarily observational and vendor-reported rather than large, independent randomized controlled trials. Real-world effectiveness can vary based on specialty, clinic workflow, hardware, and how consistently the tool is used.
sections.patient_text: For clinicians, DeepScribe is intended to shrink the amount of time spent typing notes so more time can be spent face-to-face with patients. For patients, this can mean your clinician looks at the computer less and you more, while still documenting carefully. The clinician always reviews and signs notes—DeepScribe is an assistant, not a replacement for their professional judgment.

sections.heading: Who Is DeepScribe Best For?
sections.text: DeepScribe is generally best for clinicians and practices who:
items: Spend significant time charting during or after visits and want to reduce documentation burden.
Work in outpatient or ambulatory care settings with relatively predictable visit formats.
Use an EHR that DeepScribe can integrate with (for example, major commercial EHRs via standard interfaces and BAAs).
Have reliable internet, microphones, and exam room setups that support accurate audio capture.
Are comfortable reviewing AI-generated notes and making corrections as needed before signing.
not_recommended: Clinics without stable internet or appropriate audio hardware (poor capture leads to poor notes).
Situations where recording is not legally permitted or where patient consent cannot be reliably obtained.
Clinicians who are unwilling to review and edit AI-generated notes before signing (clinical review is required).
Use as a substitute for proper risk assessment, clinical reasoning, or shared decision-making; it supports documentation only.

items.description: DeepScribe passively listens to the clinician–patient conversation using a microphone or mobile device in the exam room (or in a telehealth session). The system is designed to detect medically relevant details from natural conversation without forcing the clinician to dictate in rigid templates.
items.evidence: Ambient capture allows more natural interaction but depends on room acoustics, microphone placement, and background noise. Clinician review remains essential.

items.description: Based on the captured conversation, DeepScribe generates a structured note aligned to standard sections (for example, HPI, ROS, Past Medical History, Physical Exam, Assessment & Plan). Notes are tailored to the specialty and can be configured to match clinic preferences.
items.evidence: Standardized sections can improve readability and may support coding and quality measurement, but the note is only as accurate as the captured conversation and clinician review.

items.description: DeepScribe integrates with common EHR systems via secure connections and BAAs. Generated notes can be opened, edited, and signed within or alongside the EHR, reducing double documentation and copy-paste.
items.evidence: Tight integration can reduce clicks and improve adoption, but setup requires IT coordination and configuration specific to each health system.

items.description: The system supports multiple specialties (e.g., primary care, cardiology, orthopedics, psychiatry) with templates and note structures tuned to those workflows.
items.evidence: Specialty-tuned templates can improve perceived note relevance, but clinicians still need to adjust content to individual patient circumstances.

items.description: Clinicians can edit and approve notes before signing. Organizations can configure standard phrases, macro content, and documentation policies to align with coding and compliance requirements.
items.evidence: Human-in-the-loop review and organizational policies are key safeguards to prevent over-reliance on automation and to maintain documentation quality.

sections.heading: Privacy & Data Security
sections.summary: DeepScribe is designed as a HIPAA-compliant Business Associate with encryption, access controls, and contractual commitments not to use PHI for unrelated advertising or general-purpose AI model training. Grade: A-
items: Audio, transcripts, and notes are transmitted over encrypted connections and stored using encryption at rest.
DeepScribe operates as a HIPAA Business Associate for covered entities, with BAAs outlining permitted uses and safeguards for PHI.
Access to PHI is restricted to authorized personnel and systems required to deliver the service and support the clinic.
Documentation emphasizes that PHI from customer environments is not used to train unrelated consumer-facing models or for advertising.
Customers can request data handling details and security documentation as part of procurement and compliance review.
data_collected: Audio from clinical encounters (when enabled and consented).
Derived transcripts and notes containing PHI.
Technical logs needed to ensure reliability, security, and support.
data_shared: PHI shared with the customer’s EHR as part of clinical documentation workflows, under BAA.
De-identified or aggregated metrics may be shared internally to improve performance and reliability.
Infrastructure providers (such as cloud hosting and logging services) receive limited data necessary to operate the system, subject to contractual safeguards.
concerns: As with any ambient recording tool, there is risk if recording occurs without clear patient consent or in environments not designed for privacy.
Accuracy depends on audio quality; misheard details must be caught by clinician review before signing.
Clinics should perform their own security, legal, and compliance review, including verifying the current BAA and privacy policy.
sections.hipaa_note: DeepScribe positions itself as a HIPAA Business Associate and signs BAAs with covered entities. Clinicians and organizations remain responsible for ensuring that use of the tool complies with local laws, organizational policies, and patient consent requirements.

sections.heading: How to Start Using DeepScribe
steps: Visit deepscribe.ai and request a demo or contact the sales team to discuss your clinic’s size, specialty, and EHR setup.
Work with the DeepScribe team to confirm technical requirements, sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), and plan EHR integration.
Identify pilot clinicians or clinics who are interested in reducing documentation burden and are comfortable trying ambient scribing.
Set up hardware and software (microphones, mobile apps, or companion tools) in exam rooms or telehealth workflows.
Provide training to clinicians and staff on how visits will be recorded, how notes will appear, and how to review and sign them.
Begin a pilot period, closely monitoring note quality, clinician satisfaction, and documentation time before and after rollout.
Refine templates, workflows, and audio setups based on pilot feedback, then scale to additional clinicians or sites if results are positive.
tips: Start with a small group of motivated clinicians who are particularly burdened by documentation and open to new workflows.
Invest time in good audio: quiet rooms, reliable microphones, and clear speaking habits improve note quality.
Establish a clear process for clinicians to correct notes and report issues so the team can continuously improve.
Communicate with patients about why audio may be used and how their information is protected; obtain consent per policy.
Monitor both objective metrics (time per note, after-hours charting) and subjective metrics (burnout, satisfaction).
common_mistakes: Turning on ambient capture without clear patient consent processes and signage.
Underestimating the importance of audio quality and room setup.
Rolling out to an entire organization at once without piloting and iterating.
Assuming AI-generated notes do not need careful review; clinicians remain responsible for final content.
Failing to involve compliance, legal, and IT early in the procurement and implementation process.

faqs.a: DeepScribe is designed to operate as a HIPAA-compliant Business Associate for covered entities. The company signs Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) with health care organizations and uses encryption, access controls, and other safeguards to protect PHI. As with any vendor, your organization should review the current BAA, security documentation, and privacy policy to confirm that they meet your legal and compliance requirements.

faqs.q: Does DeepScribe replace a human medical scribe?
faqs.a: In many clinics, DeepScribe is used instead of hiring a dedicated human scribe, but it does not replace human clinical judgment. The AI generates draft notes based on the conversation, and the clinician remains responsible for reviewing, editing, and signing. Some organizations may use DeepScribe alongside limited human support, especially during rollout or for complex specialties.

faqs.q: Can DeepScribe make diagnoses or treatment recommendations?
faqs.a: No. DeepScribe is a documentation tool. It listens to the conversation and generates a note, but it does not independently diagnose, prescribe, or decide on treatment. The clinician remains fully responsible for clinical assessment, decision-making, and documentation of the care plan.

faqs.q: How does DeepScribe get into the EHR?
faqs.a: DeepScribe integrates with EHR systems through secure interfaces and configuration specific to each organization. Generated notes are typically delivered into the clinician’s EHR workspace, where they can be reviewed, edited, and signed like any other note. The exact workflow depends on the EHR vendor and the integration approach approved by your IT department.

faqs.q: What if the AI note is wrong or incomplete?
faqs.a: Clinician review is mandatory. If a note is inaccurate or incomplete, the clinician must correct it before signing. Organizations should train clinicians to treat AI-generated notes as a draft and to make sure the final signed documentation accurately reflects the encounter. If there are recurring issues, they should be reported to DeepScribe and your internal team so audio setup, templates, or workflows can be adjusted.

faqs.q: How are patients informed that a visit is being recorded?
faqs.a: Patient communication and consent practices vary by organization and local law. Many clinics use signage, verbal notification at the start of the visit, and consent forms that explain that an AI scribe is being used to support documentation. Your clinic’s legal and compliance teams should define the exact consent process and scripts that clinicians should follow.

DeepScribe is used across multiple specialties, including primary care and various medical and surgical subspecialties. The system offers specialty-tuned templates and note structures. During evaluation, organizations typically confirm that the tool performs well for their specific workflows and adjust templates as needed.

faqs.q: How much time can DeepScribe save?
faqs.a: Reported time savings vary by clinic and specialty. Vendor case studies describe meaningful reductions in documentation time and after-hours charting, but exact percentages will depend on baseline documentation burden, visit complexity, and how consistently clinicians use the tool. Many organizations evaluate DeepScribe in a pilot and measure changes in time per note, after-hours work, and clinician-reported burnout before deciding on broader rollout.

faqs.q: Does DeepScribe work for telehealth visits?
faqs.a: Yes, many ambient scribe workflows, including DeepScribe, can be used for telehealth visits as long as audio can be captured from the visit platform and the patient is informed. Your IT and clinical teams should confirm the exact setup for your telehealth platform, including how audio is routed and how consent is documented.

faqs.q: What happens if my internet connection or hardware fails?
faqs.a: DeepScribe depends on reliable audio capture and network connectivity. If internet or hardware failures occur, the system may not capture enough of the encounter to generate a useful note. Clinicians should be prepared to document using their usual EHR workflows in those situations and report recurring issues to IT and the vendor so that infrastructure can be improved.

editorial.reviewStatement: Description, workflow context, and privacy considerations for DeepScribe were reviewed against DeepScribe’s public materials and current literature on ambient clinical documentation tools as of December 2025. Because there are limited independent randomized trials for specific AI scribe platforms, all impact statements are framed at the level of vendor-reported outcomes and emerging benchmarking research rather than definitive patient-outcome data.
